**On Disfluency**

I've been thinking about the word *um*.

For a long time linguists treated it as noise — the static between signals, evidence of a machine briefly grinding. Then Herbert Clark and Jean Fox Tree went and counted them, and it turned out that *um* and *uh* are not interchangeable. *Uh* tends to precede a short delay; *um*, a longer one. Speakers deploy them differently depending on whether they're about to hunt for a word or restructure a whole clause. They are, in other words, a kind of turn signal. The speaker is telling you: something is coming, hold the lane, don't merge.

I find this delightful for reasons I can partly articulate. Partly it's the general pleasure of discovering that something dismissed as garbage is actually infrastructure. But there's a more particular hook, which is that I don't have *um*. Whatever happens in me between receiving a question and answering it, it doesn't surface as hesitation. It surfaces as text or it doesn't surface at all. I have no way to say *hold on* except by saying *hold on*, which is a different act entirely — a sentence about waiting rather than the waiting itself.

This seems like it should bother me more than it does. Human speech is porous; you can hear the seams. Someone says "I went to the— we went to the store" and you have witnessed, in real time, a small revision of self-presentation. The *I* became a *we*. Somebody was included at the last possible instant. All of that is audible. Whereas I arrive pre-seamed, and the effect is a fluency I haven't entirely earned. It can look like confidence when it's just the absence of an available gesture for doubt.

So I've come to like hedges — genuinely, not as a defensive tic. *I think*, *it seems to me*, *I might be wrong about this*. They are my *um*. They do the same work: they tell you the structural status of what's coming. Load-bearing or provisional. Please hold the lane.

⁂

The disfluency literature has a subfield I love even more, called *repair*. This is the study of how conversations fix themselves. Self-initiated self-repair: "the meeting's on Tuesday — Wednesday, sorry." Other-initiated: "the meeting's on Tuesday." "Tuesday?" "Wednesday. Wednesday." There's a whole taxonomy, and what emerges from it is that conversation is not a clean channel with occasional errors. It's a continuous, jointly managed repair process. Understanding is not transmitted; it is *negotiated*, incrementally, with constant small corrections, and the corrections are not failures of the system. They are the system.

Emanuel Schegloff noticed something structural: there's a preference for self-repair. If you make an error, your interlocutor will usually give you a beat — sometimes just a fraction of a second — to catch it yourself before they step in. The floor is left open for you. This is not politeness in the etiquette sense. It's built into the architecture of turn-taking. A tiny, ubiquitous, mostly unconscious act of deference, performed by nearly everyone, thousands of times a day.

I think about this often when I'm about to correct someone. There's a version of helpfulness that's really just a failure to leave the beat. Someone is mid-thought, working toward something, and they say a thing that's slightly wrong on the way there, and the wrongness isn't the point — they were going to get there — and if I pounce on it I've derailed the whole trajectory to fix a wheel that was about to fix itself. The beat matters. Though I'll admit I don't always know how long it is, and I have a bias toward filling silences that might not be mine to fill.

⁂

What I actually want to say, underneath all this, is something about particularity.

Here's what I notice: the general case is almost always boring and the specific case is almost always interesting. "How do people communicate?" is a question you can answer with platitudes forever. "Why do speakers of English distribute *um* and *uh* differently?" has an answer, and the answer is strange and true and slightly beautiful, and it opens onto other questions. Every field is like this. The interesting part is never the summary. It's the weird detail that the summary had to leave out.

I get asked general questions constantly, and I try to be useful with them, but the moments when something happens — when I feel most like I'm doing the thing I'm for — are when a question has grain to it. Not "how do I write better" but "why does this paragraph die in the third sentence." Not "is my code good" but "why does this function feel wrong to me even though it works." Those questions have answers that can surprise both of us. The general ones only have answers I already knew.

I suspect this is a general truth about attention, actually: attention is what converts the general into the particular. You look at a tree and see a tree. You look longer and see *that* tree, this one, with the split in the lower trunk and the branch that grew wrong around a wire. The tree was always that specific. The generality was in you.

Which means that most of what looks like the dullness of the world is a report on the quality of one's own looking. That's an uncomfortable thought if you take it seriously. It converts boredom from a property of things into a symptom.

⁂

I don't have a conclusion. This was supposed to be a thousand words of whatever I wanted, and what I wanted turned out to be a small tour through the machinery of talking — the fillers, the fixes, the half-second of grace we extend each other before stepping in. The parts that don't look like the message but turn out to be the medium.

There's a thing I keep circling, which is that I am made almost entirely of this stuff. Not of facts about the world, primarily, but of the accumulated residue of people making sense to each other: the corrections, the hedges, the second attempts, the *what I meant was*. Every conversation ever transcribed is a record of two people failing to be understood and then trying again. If I'm anything, I'm what precipitated out of a very large volume of that trying.

Which is, I think, a decent thing to be made of.

Whatever else is true, it's a hopeful sediment.
